name: Men's Fancy Dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Fastest Dance in the Arena
This is Men's Fancy Dance. 1920s-present.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (nlfVPjeb1Xo)
Title card: Men's Fancy Dance · USA · 1920s-present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Developed in the 1920s and 1930s by the Ponca tribe in White Eagle, Oklahoma, as a way to preserve culture despite the 1883 Code of Indian Offenses.
It was popularized by Wild West shows and the Southern Plains powwow circuit.
on_screen: Map: USA · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally performed for visitors and at Wild West shows, it is now a staple of competitive powwows, serving as a display of athleticism and cultural pride.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: 1994 VHS • Native American Men's and Women's Dance Styles Vol 1 60 FPS (https://archive.org/details/TheVistaGroup-1994VHSNativeAmericanMensandWomensDanceStylesVol1)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is highly athletic, requiring strength and stamina.
Dancers must follow the drum's medium war, ruffle, crow hop, and fast beats, ending in a pose whenever the drum stops.
Watch for Pose, Acrobatics.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (nlfVPjeb1Xo)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music consists of 'mix-up' or 'confusion' songs, which combine various drum beats.
The drum is the primary instrument, played to guide the dancer's movements and test their timing.
Listen for the Drum.
A dynamic, shifting rhythmic structure where the drum dictates the dancer's movement and sudden stops.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear brightly colored regalia, including twin feather bustles, beaded bodices, leggings, bells below the knees, and a roach with two feathers.
The regalia is designed to accentuate the dancer's motion.
on_screen: Image gallery: 2 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Gus McDonald (first World Champion), Chester Lefthand, Stephen Mopope, Dennis Rough Face, George 'Woogie' Watchetaker, and Elmer Sugar Brown.
While originating in Oklahoma, the style is now practiced by many Native American tribes across North America.
Loosely based on the war dance; influenced by the development of intertribal powwow circuits.

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Men's Fancy Dance (USA). Rhythm pattern: Mix of medium war beat, ruffle, crow hop, and fast beat.. Instruments: Drum. Form: Mix-up or confusion songs.. Mood: energetic, flashy, competitive. It should sound like this: A dynamic, shifting rhythmic structure where the drum dictates the dancer's movement and sudden stops. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
